result:
"Meanwhile" might be the most quietly magical word in English. It appears constantly in novels—the hero climbs the mountain, *meanwhile*, back at the village—and we glide right past it. But pause for a second: meanwhile insists that other things are happening. Right now, while you read this sentence, somewhere someone is falling asleep, someone is waking, someone is hearing news that will rearrange their entire life. The word is a tiny window into the staggering fact that existence does not wait for us. The world runs in parallel; we just happen to be standing in one of its lanes.

We live most of our lives inside a single thread, so it takes effort to remember the tapestry. Children feel this less acutely—they assume the world exists for them—but adulthood is partly the slow education in meanwhiles. The first time you visit a hospital waiting room, you understand it viscerally: hundreds of private dramas unfolding simultaneously, none more important to the universe than yours, each all-consuming from the inside.

Maybe that's what empathy really is: the trained ability to hold a meanwhile. To remember that the rude driver, the distracted barista, the friend who didn't call—all of them are mid-story, carrying plots we can't see.

Fiction teaches this better than anything else. Every novel is a machine for manufacturing parallel lives, letting us borrow consciousnesses the way we can't in reality.

So tonight, when you're brushing your teeth, try it: *meanwhile*. Feel the world hum behind the walls.
